newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's new economic team faces daunting problems.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's new economic team faces daunting problems.

text.p: South Korea's new finance minister, appointed on Wednesday, faces a host of problems from plunging exports to labour unrest and a banking crisis in Asia's wounded "tiger" economy.
But although Kang Kyong-shik will be under intense public pressure to produce a quick fix, economists said his hands will be tied in a presidential election year.

Beset by scandal -- most recently the collapse of the nation's second largest steelmaker in a loans-for-kickbacks scam -- President Kim Young-sam has picked an experienced administrator known for caution.
"In the current environment, restructuring is unlikely," said Richard Samuelson, head of research at SBC Warburg.
"After all the scandals Kim doesn't have much appetite for more confrontation. He will spend a lot of time looking after his wounds."
The president also appointed Lim Chang-yuel to take over from Ahn Kwang-koo as Minister of Trade, Industry and Energy.

A total of seven ministerial portfolios changed hands in a reshuffle designed to help restore the president's image badly damaged by the failure of Hanbo Steel Co under $5.8 billion in largely unsecured loans.
Opposition parties have accused the government of peddling influence to pressure banks into offering loans.
The affair has further exposed corrupt links between a government-directed banking system and politicians and prompted calls for urgent financial reform.
But economists said banking reform would inevitably mean massive layoffs in the industry, and Kang was unlikely to risk rising unemployment before presidential polls in December.
Although Kim is barred by the constitution from seeking a second term, he is jockeying to be kingmaker.
"You don't want people laid off in an election year," said Rhee Namuh, head of research at Dongbang Peregrine Securities.
Another immediate crisis for the new economic management team is labour reform.
President Kim was forced to return a new labour law to parliament after almost a month of wildcat strikes greeted its forced passage through parliament on December 26.

The government has now caved in on a key provision of the new law that would have made it easier for companies to lay off workers and reduce bloated costs. Debate in parliament is still raging, but political parties have promised a revised bill by Saturday.
"It's a major source of disappointment that change in the labour law has been stymied," said Samuelson.
"Flexbility in the Korean labour force will be introduced rather gradually over time. Therefore cost control will be put off longer than necessary."
Hanbo's failure and the labour strife have forced economists to revise downward their growth forecast.

In the latest gloomy assessment, the Samsung Economic Research Institute predicted Gross Domestic Product growth this year at 5.0 percent -- the weakest since 1980 -- against an earlier projection of 6.3 percent.
Growth last year was 6.9 percent.

Plunging prices of major exports, including computer chips, and rising costs of commodity imports have derailed growth. The problems have been exacerbated by a weak yen, which makes rival Japanese exports more competitive.
Kang's predecessor, Han Seung-soo, presided over a devaluation of the Korean won and an anti-consumption campaign to try to cut imports and boost exports.
Economists said the plan had backfired by fuelling inflation, raising import costs and dampening consumer demand, one of the few bright spots of the economy.
Hank Morris, managing director of Coryo Securities, said Kang "will be committed to won depreciation for as long as the yen is weak".
He added that the new minister might try to give a short-term lift to the economy before the election with large infrastructure spending.
"Spending will probably kick in during the summer in an attempt to get growth up before heading into election campaigning," Morris said.
